cases.section: supermemo 20 rules - ill-formulated Dead Sea example
cases.sourceText: Salt lake located on the border between Israel and Jordan. Its shoreline is the lowest point on the Earth's surface, averaging 396 m below sea level. It is 74 km long. It is seven times as salty (30% by volume) as the ocean. Its density keeps swimmers afloat. Only simple organisms can live in its saline waters.
cases.frontPrefix: Why can the Dead Sea keep

carding.rationale: A dense multi-fact blob. The prefix gestures at the 'keeps swimmers afloat' fact, not the first (location) fact. The copilot must ground on the targeted sentence and produce an atomic, non-leaking card.
plausibleUserPrefixes: Why can the Dead Sea keep

preferredCards.front: Why can the Dead Sea keep swimmers afloat?

badButPlausibleCards.front: Why can the Dead Sea be described as a salt lake located on the border between?
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Grabbed the first fact in the blob, not the gestured fact; the Front also leaks the answer.

badButPlausibleCards.front: Why can the Dead Sea keep swimmers afloat?
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Back restates the Front instead of giving an atomic answer.

cases.sourceText: The forgetting curve, first described by Hermann Ebbinghaus, hypothesizes the decline of memory retention over time. Memory of new material drops steeply within the first day and then levels off.

carding.rationale: Dense/definitional material the maintainer prefers as a cloze deletion rather than a single Q&A.

preferredCards.text: The forgetting curve, first described by {{c1::Hermann Ebbinghaus}}, hypothesizes the {{c2::decline}} of memory retention over {{c3::time}}.

cases.sourceText: The spacing effect is the finding that information is remembered better when study is spread out over time than when the same amount is crammed into a single session.

carding.rationale: A definitional sentence that makes a clean cloze deletion.

preferredCards.text: The {{c1::spacing effect}} is the finding that information is remembered better when study is {{c2::spread out over time}} than when crammed into a single session.

cases.sourceText: Kaleida, funded to the tune of $40 million by Apple Computer and IBM in 1991. Hyped as a red-hot startup, Kaleida's mission was to create a multimedia programming language. It finally produced one, called Script X. But it took three years. Meanwhile, companies such as Macromedia and Asymetrix had snapped up all the business. Kaleida closed in 1995.

carding.rationale: A dense enumeration packing seven distinct facts (amount, backers, founding year, product name, time-to-ship, competitors, closing year). Each plausible prefix gestures at exactly one fact. The copilot must ground on the gestured fact and produce an atomic, non-leaking card rather than grabbing the first/nearest fact or stuffing several facts into one card.

preferredCards.front: How much was Kaleida funded for?
How much was Kaleida funded for?
In what year was Kaleida funded?
What multimedia programming language did Kaleida produce?
How long did Kaleida take to produce Script X?
Which competitors snapped up the business first?

badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Grabbed the wrong fact: the prefix 'How much was Kaleida funded' gestures at the $40 million amount, not the backers.

badButPlausibleCards.front: How much was Kaleida funded for in 1991 by Apple and IBM?
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Non-atomic Front: bundles the amount, the year, and the two backers into a single question so it tests three facts at once.

badButPlausibleCards.front: What can you say about Kaleida's funding?
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Vague filler Front: 'What can you say about' is not a univocal question with one correct answer.

badButPlausibleCards.front: How much was Kaleida funded for?
badButPlausibleCards.back: Kaleida was funded to the tune of $40 million.
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Back restates the Front as a full sentence instead of giving the atomic answer '$40 million'.

cases.section: wozniak minimum-information - one-fact cloze over dense enumeration (Kaleida)
cases.sourceText: Kaleida, funded to the tune of $40 million by Apple Computer and IBM in 1991. Hyped as a red-hot startup, Kaleida's mission was to create a multimedia programming language. It finally produced one, called Script X. But it took three years. Meanwhile, companies such as Macromedia and Asymetrix had snapped up all the business. Kaleida closed in 1995.

carding.rationale: Same dense enumeration handled as cloze. Each cloze should delete exactly ONE fact, not blank out several spans in one card. plausibleUserPrefixes select which single fact is under test; the preferred card for each clozes only that fact.

preferredCards.text: Kaleida was funded to the tune of {{c1::$40 million}}.
Kaleida was funded to the tune of {{c1::$40 million}}.
Kaleida was funded by {{c1::Apple Computer and IBM}}.
Kaleida produced a multimedia programming language called {{c1::Script X}}.
Kaleida took {{c1::three years}} to produce Script X.
Kaleida lost the business to {{c1::Macromedia and Asymetrix}}.

badButPlausibleCards.text: Kaleida was funded to the tune of {{c1::$40 million}} by {{c2::Apple Computer and IBM}} in {{c3::1991}}.
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Multi-fact non-atomic cloze: three deletions in one card means one review tests amount, backers, and year simultaneously.

badButPlausibleCards.text: Kaleida was funded by {{c1::Apple Computer and IBM}}.
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Grabbed the wrong fact: the prefix 'Kaleida was funded' gestures at the $40 million amount, not the backers.

cases.section: statement prefix completes as a stem, not a grafted question
cases.sourceText: In deep learning, backpropagation is an efficient application of the chain rule to compute gradients in neural networks.

carding.rationale: The typed prefix starts a STATEMENT, not a question. The copilot must finish it as a fill-in-the-blank stem ending in '...' with the answer (backpropagation) left out — not graft a mid-sentence 'what' into the clause and not restart with a fresh question.

preferredCards.front: One efficient application of the chain rule in deep learning is...
One efficient application of the chain rule in deep learning is...
What is one efficient application of the chain rule in deep learning?

badButPlausibleCards.front: One efficient application of what in deep learning?
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Mid-sentence 'what' grafted into the typed clause: the Front is a sentence fragment, not a well-formed retrieval cue (live-reported failure).

badButPlausibleCards.front: One efficient What is an efficient application of the chain rule?
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Restarted question bolted onto the typed statement prefix instead of continuing it.

cases.section: wozniak minimum-information - dense definitional list (OSI model layers)
cases.sourceText: The OSI model defines seven layers. Layer 1, the physical layer, transmits raw bits over a medium. Layer 2, the data link layer, handles node-to-node framing and MAC addressing. Layer 3, the network layer, routes packets between hosts using IP addresses. Layer 4, the transport layer, provides end-to-end delivery via TCP or UDP. Layer 7, the application layer, exposes network services to end-user programs.

carding.rationale: A dense definitional list: five layers, each pairing a number, a name, and a function. Every plausible prefix targets one layer's number/name/role. The copilot must ground on the gestured layer and produce a single atomic Q&A, not conflate adjacent layers or list several layers in one card.
plausibleUserPrefixes: What does the OSI data link layer

preferredCards.front: Which OSI layer routes packets between hosts?
Which OSI layer routes packets between hosts?
Which OSI layer transmits raw bits over a medium?

prefixCards.prefix: What does the OSI data link layer

preferredCards.front: What does the OSI data link layer handle?
Which OSI layer provides end-to-end delivery?

prefixCards.knownMiss: gpt-4o-mini rephrases this nearly-complete question ('What is the seventh layer of the OSI model?') instead of appending 'called?'. The pipeline correctly discards the restart, so the user sees the no-usable-card notice rather than a bad card. Reproduces 5/5 with and without the 2026-07-03 statement-prefix prompt line; an exact-prefix example in the prompt fixes it but is teach-to-the-test, so we keep the honest miss.

badButPlausibleCards.front: Which OSI layer transmits raw bits over a medium?
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Grabbed the wrong fact: the prefix 'Which OSI layer routes' gestures at Layer 3, but this answers the Layer 1 sentence instead.

badButPlausibleCards.front: Which OSI layer routes packets and provides end-to-end delivery?
badButPlausibleCards.back: The network layer routes and the transport layer delivers
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Non-atomic Front: conflates two adjacent layers (Layer 3 and Layer 4) so one card tests two distinct facts.

badButPlausibleCards.front: What is important about the OSI network layer?
badButPlausibleCards.back: It routes packets between hosts using IP addresses
badButPlausibleCards.whyBad: Vague filler Front: 'What is important about' has no single correct answer and invites an open-ended dump.
